To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the decay of higher-order resonances can be neglected in event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions.

resonance decays are important for anisotropic flow calculations and that partial resonance calculations provide good approximations for single particle spectra and higher-order anisotropy coefficients.

the resonance decay contributions to the anisotropic flow can be well described by the leading-order hydrodynamic calculations, and the partial resonance decay simulations with fewer species of particles can reproduce the flow results from full resonance simulations with a good level of accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and implementation of new techniques for the simulation of relativistic heavy ion collisions.
a systematic analysis of resonance decay contributions to higher order flow coefficients in hydrodynamics.
the development and application of a new method for resonance decay calculations in hydrodynamic simulations of relativistic heavy ion collisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the resonance decays have an impact on the flow anisotropy, especially at high p T, and the impact is stronger for the higher-order harmonics.
the partial resonance decay approach is a good choice for the study of higher order flow coefficients.
the strong resonance decay contributions to higher order flow harmonics are small and negligible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the partial resonance calculation is a reliable and efficient tool for studying the collective flow in relativistic heavy-ion physics.
resonance decay calculations can now be done in large scale hydrodynamic simulations for heavy-ion collisions.
the resonance decays are important for the flow anisotropy of particles at low pT and the resonance decay contributions are not negligible in high pT flow anisotroies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the resonance decay contributions to higher order flow coefficients can be well described by a few resonance decays, which are dominated by the decay of the $\Delta(1232)$ resonance.
in hydrodynamic calculations of heavy-ion collisions the flow coefficients of resonance decays can be approximated by a superposition of the decay products' flow coefficients.
the anisotropic flows are dominated by particles that have a large mass, and that are not strongly coupled.
